title: the mouth full of universe
carry: a little dirt on his lips

segments.voice: Last week ended with the butter thief dragging a mortar between two trees, and two cursed brothers walking free. Your line was two trees fall, two men go free. What was within reach, right where you were stuck? Day eight hundred ninety.

Mother, Krishna ate dirt! The other boys come running to tell on him, his older brother Balarama among them. Small children put things in their mouths, and this one has just put a handful of earth in his. Yashoda grabs him by the hand, scolds him, and asks why. And the little boy, standing there with dirt on his lips, looks his mother in the eye and denies everything. Today, a toddler's lie, and a very strange answer to it.

His defense is simple. I didn't eat any dirt, Mother. They're lying. If you think they're telling the truth, look in my mouth yourself. So he opens it, and she looks in. And there, inside her son's mouth, she sees everything. The Bhagavata lists it, as if it can hardly stop: the sky and the directions, the mountains, the islands and the oceans, the whole round earth, the wind and fire, the moon and the stars. The turning of time. The gods. The elements that make up a body, and the mind itself. And then, in among all of it, she sees the village of Vraja. And in the village, she sees herself. Where does that put her? She's standing in her yard looking into her son's mouth, and inside his mouth she finds her yard, and herself standing in it. The text doesn't let her off easily. She's frightened. She asks: is this a dream? Is this some illusion sent by God? Is my own mind confused? Or is it some power that belongs to my child? She doesn't know what to call it. So she does the only thing that seems to fit. She bows, inwardly, to the one who is beyond all thought, in whom all of this rests. Here is what the story is saying. The baby she nurses, the boy she ties to a mortar, the one who steals the neighbors' butter, holds everything that is. Not as a picture of it. All of it, her included. And the doorway to that vision is a small boy's open mouth, with a little dirt on his lips.
screen: `"LOOK IN MY MOUTH."` · `SKY, MOUNTAINS, OCEANS, STARS.` · `THE VILLAGE, AND HERSELF IN IT.` · then, large: `A DREAM, OR GOD, OR MY CHILD?`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your eyes close or rest low. Start with what's closest: your breath, moving in and out. Then widen. The room around you. The building, the street. The town, the land, the sea beyond it. The sky over all of it, and the stars past the sky. Hold that as wide as you can for a few breaths. Then let it come back to your breath again, and notice that you're inside all of it, the way Yashoda saw herself inside the vision. If you pray, you can rest in prayer here. The bell holds the time.
Yashoda. Krishna's mother, who looks into her son's mouth for dirt, and finds everything, and herself.
Your line: a little dirt on his lips. Today, look closely at one ordinary small thing, and let it be bigger than you expected. Day eight hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Krishna devotees tell this story alongside the butter-thief stories, and devotional paintings and songs show Yashoda peering into the child's open mouth.
